subject: mathematics
question_text: If b + c = 3a, find the value of cot(B/2) cot(C/2).

mark_split.label: Write the product of the two cotangents

steps.label: Write the product of the two cotangents
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. The product of the two cotangents leaves s/(s−a) — the bracket of the angle that was NOT used.
steps.memory_tip: cot(B/2) cot(C/2) = s/(s−a) — the bracket left is the one for the angle not used.
lines: = s/(s−a)   [∵ s > a, both are positive]

recall.must_convey: That cot(B/2) cot(C/2) = s/(s−a), because (s−b) and (s−c) cancel between the two roots.
accept: multiply the two half angle cotangents and s minus b and s minus c cancel
the product is s over s minus a
the bracket left over is the one for the angle not used
rendu cotangents multiply cheste s by s minus a vasthundi
the product of cot half B and cot half C is s over s minus a

steps.why: Multiplying the two roots cancels (s−b) and (s−c) completely and leaves s over the bracket of the angle that was not asked for. That is why the answer depends only on a.
common_mistakes: Writing cot(B/2) cot(C/2) = s/(s−b) or s/(s−c).
Adding the two cotangents instead of multiplying them.

steps.label: Use b + c = 3a
steps.margin_note: The other mark. 2s = a + (b+c) = 4a gives s = 2a, so s − a = a and the ratio is 2a/a = 2.
steps.memory_tip: 2s = a + (b + c) = a + 3a = 4a, so s = 2a and s − a = a; the ratio is 2.

recall.must_convey: That b + c = 3a gives 2s = 4a, so s = 2a, s − a = a and s/(s−a) = 2.
accept: two s is a plus b plus c which is four a so s is two a
then s minus a is a and the ratio is two
the a cancels so the answer is a plain two
two s equals four a kabatti s equals two a, answer two
substitute b plus c equals three a into the perimeter

steps.why: The given relation fixes the perimeter as 4a, so s = 2a and s − a = a. The ratio s/(s−a) is then a pure number and a drops out, which is why no side lengths are needed.
common_mistakes: Writing s = a + b + c instead of 2s = a + b + c.
Substituting b + c = 3a into b and c separately.
